title: Jim's anomaly hunt: 234 short-term tests, is each one random, and how fast does it fade?

claims.claim: With enough data you can tell an anomaly is not random
claims.test: OOS hit rate (OOS t >= 2, same sign) by how strong the in-sample proof was
claims.result: IS t 2-3: 9/35 held (25.7%); IS t 3-5: 4/19 held (21.1%); IS t 5-10: 6/19 held (31.6%); IS t 10+: 6/9 held (66.7%). Passed all 3 randomness checks: 13/31 held (41.9%). Naive but failed FDR: 8/25.

claims.test: Share of the in-sample effect (bp) still there OOS, for all FDR passers; exponential fit on quarterly bp
claims.result: median edge kept OOS = 0.12 of in-sample (n 57); survivors median half-life 1.59 years, 3 of 13 survivors show no fade; Spearman(IS t, fade speed k) = +0.19 (p 0.17, n 57); Spearman(IS bp, share of edge kept OOS) = +0.25 (p 0.06)

claims.test: Survivors (not random + held OOS) that are still positive after costs, OOS
claims.result: 13 survived; 0 beat taker costs (14 bp crypto round trip), 2 beat maker costs (4 bp)

takeaways: Moon Dev ran 224 pre-declared short-term tests. 82 looked real in-sample (|t| >= 2). 38 passed Bonferroni, 57 passed FDR, 31 passed FDR + deflated Sharpe + shuffle test. 13 held out-of-sample. 0 beat taker costs.
Jim is right that more proof means more real: tests with IS t 10+ held OOS 66.7% of the time, tests with t 2-3 only 25.7%. Passing all 3 randomness checks lifted the hit rate from 30.5% to 41.9%.

Jim's 'persisted long enough' rule works as a number: t >= 2 in EVERY one of 4 in-sample chunks held OOS 56.2% vs 24.2% for pooled-only. That is the best single filter here. Just 'same sign every chunk' did not help.

Jim is right that they fade: the median FDR passer kept only 12% of its in-sample bp out-of-sample. Median survivor half-life 1.6 years. The strongest ones did NOT clearly fade faster (Spearman(IS t, fade speed k) = +0.19 (p 0.17, n 57); Spearman(IS bp, share of edge kept OOS) = +0.25 (p 0.06)).

Top 3 survivors: A_CRV_1m_lastbar (fade) OOS +6.83 bp gross, -7.17 bp after taker, +2.83 bp after maker, OOS t 42.0, 1 tick = 23.75 bp; J_CRV_5m_takerimb (fade) OOS +1.06 bp gross, -12.94 bp after taker, -2.94 bp after maker, OOS t 4.0, 1 tick = 23.75 bp; B_CRV_5m_lastbar (fade) OOS +4.50 bp gross, -9.50 bp after taker, +0.50 bp after maker, OOS t 27.5, 1 tick = 23.75 bp.

The top survivors are bid-ask bounce, not alpha: CRV's tick is about 24 bp of price OOS, so a 'fade the last 1m bar' effect of 6.8 bp is a quarter of one tick. Its edge GREW OOS only because CRV's price fell, making each tick bigger in bp.
BTC lead-lag (BTC moves, alt follows next 1m) is real and persistent on 8 alts, but it is 0.05 to 0.35 bp per trade vs a 14 bp taker round trip: 40x to 270x too small.

Funding extremes, liquidation spikes, hour of day, day of week, US session and every TSLA test failed the randomness checks. Liquidation spikes (SOL, XRP) passed FDR in-sample but not the shuffle test or OOS t >= 2.

Spreads and liquidity: median coin spread proxy 3.79 bp (2020) -> 0.47 bp (2025), trades per minute 72 -> 540. Real BTC perp quoted spread 0.035 bp (Aug 2023) -> 0.015 bp (Mar 2024). The proxy is noisy on BTC (it picks up volatility).
What the video leaves out: which shorter-term approaches, what 'persisted long enough' means, how fast anomalies fade. Every one of those numbers here is Moon Dev's own test, not Jim's.
